                         Direct Testimony of Robert R. Stephens

 1   I. INTRODUCTION

 2   Q   PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME AND BUSINESS ADDRESS.

 3   A   Robert R. Stephens. My business address is 16690 Swingley Ridge Road,

 4       Suite 140, Chesterfield, MO 63017.



 5   Q   WHAT IS YOUR OCCUPATION?

 6   A   I am a consultant in the field of public utility regulation and a Senior

 7       Principal with the firm of Brubaker & Associates, Inc. (“BAI”), energy,

 8       economic and regulatory consultants.



 9   Q   PLEASE        DESCRIBE           YOUR         EDUCATIONAL           AND

10       PROFESSIONAL BACKGROUND.

11   A   This information is included as Appendix A to my testimony.



12   Q   ON WHOSE BEHALF ARE YOU APPEARING IN THIS

13       PROCEEDING?

14   A   I am appearing on behalf of the Regents of the New Mexico State University

15       (“NMSU”).




                                       Page 1
                            Direct Testimony of Robert R. Stephens
                              NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1   Q    WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR TESTIMONY IN THIS

 2        PROCEEDING?

 3   A    In my testimony, I address the jurisdictional and customer class cost of

 4        service (“COS”) studies provided by El Paso Electric Company (“EPE” or

 5        “Company”). In particular, I focus on the classification and allocation of

 6        production plant in service costs. I generally support the classification and

 7        allocation methods proposed by EPE. I also comment briefly on the need

 8        for a revenue allocation which reflects moderation in light of a potentially

 9        large overall revenue increase, if one is approved.

10                I will begin by providing an overview of COS studies and their role

11        in the rate setting process.



12   II. COST OF SERVICE

13   Q    PLEASE EXPLAIN THE BASIC STEPS FOR ESTABLISHMENT

14        OF FAIR AND REASONABLE RATES?

15   A    The ratemaking process has three steps. First, we must determine the

16        utility’s total revenue requirement and whether an increase or decrease in

17        revenues is necessary. Second, we must determine how any increase or

18        decrease in revenues is to be distributed among the various customer

19        classes, i.e., the class revenue allocation. A determination of how many



                                          Page 2
                       Direct Testimony of Robert R. Stephens
                         NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1   dollars of revenue should be produced by each class is essential in obtaining

 2   the appropriate level of rates. Finally, individual tariffs must be designed

 3   to produce the required amount of revenues from each class of service and

 4   to send efficient price signals to customers.

 5           The guiding principle at each step should be COS. In the first

 6   step – determining revenue requirements – it is widely agreed that the utility

 7   is entitled to an increase only to the extent that its actual COS has increased.

 8   If current rate levels produce revenues which exceed the revenue

 9   requirement, a rate reduction is required. In short, rate revenues should

10   equal a utility’s actual COS. The same principle should apply in the last

11   two steps of establishing fair and reasonable rates. Each customer class

12   should, to the extent practicable, produce revenues equal to the cost of

13   serving that particular class. On some occasions, this may require a rate

14   increase for some customer classes and a rate decrease for others. The

15   standard tool for determining whether a class requires a rate increase or

16   decrease is an embedded class COS study, which shows the rate of return

17   for each class of service. Ideally, rate levels should be modified so that each

18   customer class provides approximately the same rate of return. Finally, in

19   designing individual tariffs, the goal is to base the rate design on the COS




                                     Page 3
                           Direct Testimony of Robert R. Stephens
                             NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1       so that each customer’s rate tracks, to the extent practicable, the utility’s

 2       cost of providing service to the customers on the tariff.



 3   Q   WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF A COS STUDY?

 4   A   The basic purpose of a COS study is an empirical determination of the cost

 5       of serving jurisdictions or classes of customers. Focusing on class COS

 6       studies, after determining the overall system cost of service or “revenue

 7       requirement,” a COS study is used to ascertain the cost of serving each of

 8       the customer classes, i.e., a COS study shows how each customer class

 9       contributes to the total system cost.

10               For example, when a class produces the same rate of return as the

11       total system, it is returning to the utility revenues just sufficient to cover the

12       costs incurred in serving it (including a reasonable authorized return on

13       investment). If a class produces a below-average rate of return, it may be

14       concluded that the revenues are insufficient to cover all relevant costs. On

15       the other hand, if a class produces a rate of return above the average, it is

16       paying revenues sufficient to cover the cost attributable to it and, in

17       addition, is paying part of the cost attributable to other classes who produce

18       a below average rate of return. The COS study is important because it




                                          Page 4
                          Direct Testimony of Robert R. Stephens
                            NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


1        shows the class revenue requirement, as well as the rate of return under

2        current and sometimes proposed rates.



3    Q   PLEASE COMMENT ON THE PROPER FUNDAMENTALS OF A

4        COS STUDY.

5    A   In all COS studies, certain fundamental concepts should be recognized. Of

6        primary importance among these concepts is the functionalization of costs,

 7       as well as the classification of the nature of these costs as to whether they

 8       vary with the quantity of energy consumed, the demand placed upon the

 9       system, or the number of customers being served. Stated another way,

10       functionalization is the determination and arrangement of costs according

11       to major functions, such as production, transmission, and distribution.

12              Fixed costs are those costs which tend to remain constant over the

13       short run irrespective of changes in output and generally are considered to

14       be demand- or customer-related. Fixed costs include those costs which are

15       a function of the size of the investment in utility facilities, and those costs

16       necessary to keep the facilities “on-line.” Variable costs, on the other hand,

17       are those costs which tend to vary with output and generally are considered

18       to be commodity-related. Customer-related costs are those which are more




                                         Page 5
                            Direct Testimony of Robert R. Stephens
                              NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1        closely related to the number of customers served, rather than the quantity

 2        of energy consumed or the peak demands placed upon the system.

 3               Once costs have been functionalized to the major utility functions,

 4        and classified by the underlying cause of incurrence, such as peak demand,

 5        the final step is allocation. In the allocation step, the cost analyst seeks the

 6        best measure or representation of the classification variable, e.g.,

 7        12 coincident peaks (“CP”), 4 CP, or 1 CP, for demand.

 8               An understanding of these concepts is essential to COS studies, as

 9        well as appropriate rate design.



10   III. REVIEW OF EPE’S COS STUDIES

11   Q    HAVE YOU REVIEWED THE COMPANY’S COS STUDIES?

12   A    Yes, I have. The COS studies are addressed in the direct testimony of

13        Adrian Hernandez. Mr. Hernandez addresses production plant in service

14        costs in two sections of his testimony; first, in regard to the jurisdictional

15        COS study at page 18, and for the class COS study at page 51.

16        Mr. Hernandez explains that while EPE has implemented a new regulatory

17        software solution to prepare its COS studies, the overall methodology of the

18        COS model has not changed.1 Mr. Hernandez indicates that EPE continues



          1
          Direct testimony of Adrian Hernandez at pages 9-12.

                                            Page 6
                          Direct Testimony of Robert R. Stephens
                            NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1       to use the National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners

 2       (“NARUC”) “Electric Utility Cost Allocation Manual” (“NARUC

 3       Manual”) as a general guide for its COS studies.



 4   Q   HOW DOES EPE CLASSIFY AND ALLOCATE PRODUCTION

 5       PLANT COSTS?

 6   A   As explained at pages 18 and 51 of Mr. Hernandez’s testimony, for the

 7       jurisdictional COS study and class COS studies, respectively, EPE classifies

 8       peaking generation plant-in-service costs as demand-related and allocates

 9       them using a 4 CP demand allocator. For other generation plant-in-service

10       costs, EPE uses a classification that develops a weighted allocation based

11       on capacity to serve average demand or energy generation, and additional

12       capacity that is needed to ensure service reliability.    Specifically, the

13       allocation is the Average and Excess (“A&E”), with 4 CP as the demand

14       measure for the excess portion, and the average portion based on annual

15       average demand, with load factor used as the weighting factor between the

16       two portions.




                                        Page 7
                          Direct Testimony of Robert R. Stephens
                            NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1   Q   IN     YOUR        OPINION,         ARE       THESE         REASONABLE

 2       CLASSIFICATION           AND      ALLOCATION             METHODS        FOR

 3       PRODUCTION PLANT-IN-SERVICE?

 4   A   Yes. EPE is a strongly summer-peaking utility, as demonstrated clearly and

 5       visually in Mr. Hernandez’s Exhibit AH-1, which shows the peak demand

 6       levels in each month, both for the single test year as well as averages over

 7       several multi-year periods. Although an argument could be made that a

 8       3 CP allocator, using June, July and August, might be more appropriate for

 9       capturing the peak demand needs, in this case, a 4 CP allocator is

10       acceptable. In my experience, a 4 CP allocator is more commonly used than

11       a 3 CP allocation factor. Further, I would not expect a significant difference

12       in allocation factors utilizing 3 CP rather than 4 CP. As such, a 4 CP

13       allocator is an appropriate representation of peak demands to be covered by

14       generating capacity.

15              A demand-based classification is accepted for such costs in the

16       NARUC Manual, and 4 CP falls within the accepted measures of peak

17       demand.2

18              Likewise, an A&E classification is also reasonable for the other

19       generation facilities, recognizing that such facilities are installed for more



         2
         NARUC Manual at pages 41-48.

                                         Page 8
                            Direct Testimony of Robert R. Stephens
                              NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1       sustained service. A&E is used in several jurisdictions within the industry,

 2       and, like a peak demand classification, is included in the NARUC Manual.3



 3   Q   IN SUMMARY, DO YOU SUPPORT EPE’S COS STUDY AS IT

 4       PERTAINS TO PRODUCTION PLANT COSTS?

 5   A   Yes.



 6   Q   DO YOU HAVE DISAGREEMENT WITH THE CLASSIFICATION

 7       AND       ALLOCATION            METHODS           FOR      OTHER      COST

 8       CATEGORIES WITHIN EPE’S COS STUDY?

 9   A   Not at this time. As indicated, my focus has been on production plant costs.

10       My review of classification and allocation of other plant cost categories has

11       not exposed any problems, but I reserve the right to comment on other

12       aspects as may be raised by other parties.




         3
         Id. at pages 49-52.

                                          Page 9
                                 Direct Testimony of Robert R. Stephens
                                   NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1   IV. REVENUE ALLOCATION

 2   Q       WHAT IS MEANT BY REVENUE ALLOCATION IN A UTILITY

 3           RATE CASE?

 4   A       Revenue allocation, sometimes called “revenue spread” is the determination

 5           of how much of the revenue requirement should be recovered from each of

 6           the rate classes. The revenue allocation should be informed by the COS

 7           study results, but also should take into consideration important ratemaking

 8           concepts like continuity, moderation, and avoidance of rate shock. These

 9           considerations can sometimes justify temporary deviation from strict

10           adherence to COS study results.



11   Q       WHICH EPE WITNESS ADDRESSES REVENUE ALLOCATION?

12   A       This is addressed by EPE witness Manuel Carrasco, at pages 5-11 of his

13           direct testimony, and by EPE witness George Novela, at pages 58-63 of his

14           direct testimony. These witnesses propose a revenue allocation that reaches

15           full cost of service for each of the classes by the proposed second step

16           increase, as determined by Company witness Hernandez’ COS study

17           results.4




             4
               Direct testimony of Manuel Carrasco at pages 5-6 and direct testimony of George Novela
     at pages 59-60.

                                                Page 10
                                   Direct Testimony of Robert R. Stephens
                                     NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1   Q          DO    THESE        WITNESSES           RECOGNIZE           THE      NEED       FOR

 2              MODERATION IN THE REVENUE ALLOCATION?

 3   A          Yes. As Mr. Novela states, “EPE recognizes that a 50.5% increase in base

 4              rate revenues in one step would place significant financial and affordability

 5              pressures on its customers, particularly residential customers, and thus is

 6              voluntarily proposing the phasing of the increase in two parts for certain,

 7              specified customer classes.”5 However, both witnesses also recognize that

 8              deviations from COS study results introduce the need for class cross-

 9              subsidization.6



10   Q          HOW DOES EPE PROPOSE TO IMPLEMENT MODERATION?

11   A          EPE’s proposal is to phase in the revenue increase for Rate Class Nos. 01,

12              05, 10B, 12, 25, and 26 over two steps. This would temporarily moderate

13              the increase to most of the rate classes which would receive increases

14              greater than the proposed system average increase of 50.5%.7 However, by

15              Phase 2, some rate classes would receive increases of as high as about 80%

16              over present rates.8



                5
                Direct testimony of George Novela at page 60.
                6
                Direct testimony of Manuel Carrasco at page 6 and direct testimony of George Novela at
     page 62.
                7
                Direct testimony of Manuel Carrasco at pages 7-8.
                8
                Id., at page 8, Table MC-1.

                                                  Page 11
                          Direct Testimony of Robert R. Stephens
                            NMPRC Docket No. 25-00082-UT


 1   Q   DO YOU AGREE THAT RATE MODERATION MAY BE NEEDED

 2       IN THIS CASE?

 3   A   Yes, especially at an overall rate increase of 50.5% as proposed by EPE by

 4       Phase 2 of its proposed increase. Normally, when it is needed, I might

 5       recommend a rate moderation target of no more than 1.5 times the system

 6       average increase. However, in this case, at such a large overall increase

 7       level, that standard would suggest a cap of nearly 76%, which most would

 8       argue is not sufficient moderation.



 9   Q   DO YOU HAVE A RECOMMENDATION?

10   A   Yes. If the Commission grants EPE an increase of anywhere near the level

11       requested, it should seriously consider something closer to an across-the-

12       board or equal percentage increase. While this could extend existing class

13       cross-subsidies, as EPE alleges, it may be necessary in the interest of rate

14       moderation under these circumstances.



15   Q   DOES THIS CONCLUDE YOUR DIRECT TESTIMONY?

16   A   Yes, it does.

                              Qualifications of Robert R. Stephens

 1   Q   PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME AND BUSINESS ADDRESS.

 2   A   Robert R. Stephens. My business address is 16690 Swingley Ridge Road, Suite 140,

 3       Chesterfield, MO 63017.



 4   Q   PLEASE STATE YOUR OCCUPATION.

 5   A   I am a consultant in the field of public utility regulation and a Senior Principal with the

 6       firm of Brubaker & Associates, Inc. (“BAI”), energy, economic and regulatory

 7       consultants.



 8   Q   PLEASE         STATE      YOUR        EDUCATIONAL             BACKGROUND             AND

 9       EXPERIENCE.

10   A   I graduated from Southern Illinois University at Carbondale in 1984 with a Bachelor of

11       Science degree in Engineering. During college, I was employed by Central Illinois

12       Public Service Company in the Gas Department. Upon graduation, I accepted a position

13       as a Mechanical Engineer at the Illinois Department of Energy and Natural Resources.

14       In the summer of 1986, I accepted a position as Energy Planner with City Water, Light

15       and Power, a municipal electric and water utility in Springfield, Illinois. My duties

16       centered on integrated resource planning and the design and administration of load

17       management programs.

18              From July 1989 to June 1994, I was employed as a Senior Economic Analyst in

19       the Planning and Operations Department of the Staff of the Illinois Commerce




                                     BRUBAKER & ASSOCIATES, INC.
                                                                                                Appendix A
                                                                                        Robert R. Stephens
                                                                                                    Page 2




1             Commission. In this position, I reviewed utility filings and prepared various reports and

2             testimony for use by the Commission. From June 1994 to August 1997, I worked as an

3             advisor to one of the Commissioners. In this role, I provided technical and policy

4             analyses on a broad spectrum of issues related to the electric, gas, telecommunications

5             and water utility industries.

6                     In May 1996, I graduated from the University of Illinois at Springfield with a

7             Master of Business Administration degree.

8                     In August 1997, I joined Brubaker & Associates, Inc. as a Consultant. Since

9             that time, I have participated in the analysis of various utility rate and restructuring

10            matters in several states and the evaluation of power supply proposals for clients. Over

11            time, I advanced to my current position.

12                    The firm of Brubaker & Associates, Inc. provides consulting services in the field

13            of energy procurement and public utility regulation to many clients, including large

14            industrial and institutional customers, some utilities, and on occasion, state regulatory

15            agencies. More specifically, we provide analysis of energy procurement options based

16            on consideration of prices and reliability as related to the needs of the client; prepare

17            rate, feasibility, economic and cost of service studies relating to energy and utility

18            services; prepare depreciation and feasibility studies relating to utility service; assist in

19            contract negotiations for utility services; and provide technical support to legislative

20            activities.
